content: Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) occurs when a newborn inhales a mixture of meconium and amniotic fluid into the lungs during or around the time of delivery. This condition can lead to significant respiratory distress. Currently, aside from supportive care, there are limited effective treatment options available for MAS. Lung lavage has been proposed as a potential therapeutic intervention, as it may help remove meconium from the airways and potentially alter the progression of the disease. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of lung lavage on morbidity and mortality in newborns diagnosed with MAS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to December 2012. Additional sources, such as previous reviews, conference proceedings, and expert consultations, were also utilized. The search included terms such as meconium aspiration, pulmonary surfactants, fluorocarbons, bronchoalveolar lavage, lung lavage, and pulmonary lavage. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the effects of lung lavage in newborns with MAS. Lung lavage was defined as a procedure involving the instillation of fluid into the lungs, followed by its removal through suctioning and/or postural drainage. Data were extracted from the included studies to assess clinical outcomes such as mortality, the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), incidence of pneumothorax, duration of mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy, length of hospital stay, pulmonary function indices, and adverse effects of the lavage procedure. Data analysis adhered to the standards of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Only four small RCTs met the inclusion criteria for this review. However, one of these trials did not provide data for the control group. Two studies compared lung lavage using diluted surfactant with standard care. A meta-analysis of these two studies did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in mortality (relative risk [RR] 0.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.12 to 1.46; risk difference [RD] -0.10, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.04) or the need for ECMO (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.04 to 1.86; RD -0.15, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.04). However, for the combined outcome of death or the need for ECMO, a significant benefit was observed in the lavage group (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.96; RD -0.19, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.03), with a number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB) of 5. No other significant benefits were reported. Another study compared surfactant lavage followed by a surfactant bolus with surfactant bolus therapy alone in cases of MAS complicated by pulmonary hypertension. This study did not show significant improvements in mortality, incidence of pneumothorax, duration of mechanical ventilation, or length of hospital stay. In conclusion, lung lavage with diluted surfactant may offer some benefit in newborns with MAS, particularly in reducing the combined outcome of death or the need for ECMO. However, the evidence is limited, and further well-designed controlled clinical trials are necessary to confirm these findings. Future studies should aim to refine the lavage technique, compare it with other treatment modalities such as surfactant bolus therapy, and evaluate long-term outcomes in affected infants.
